scripts.hook: One line from an old handbook.
scripts.hook_b: Is it possible to read a whole Stoic handbook in 7 days?
cards: One line from an old handbook.
Written down by a student around 100 AD. It opens like this:
Some things are up to you?
Today's job: one worry, two columns. Mine. Not mine.
Cross out the second column. Out loud if you like.
Reply DONE. Day 2 opens with how many of you did it.
scripts.visual: Same pocket book on the same desk every day of the series; hand draws one tally mark at the end. Counter 'DAY 1/7' top third in Ember. V1 Slate + grain if no footage.
scripts.caption:
Day 1 of 7.

Epictetus never wrote a book. A student, Arrian, took notes and later boiled them down into a pocket handbook. This is how it opens: some things are up to us, some aren't.

Today: take one worry. Two columns, mine and not mine. Cross out the second.

Reply DONE (or comment it). Tomorrow's post opens with the real count.

Which column is bigger?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Moodius: mine had one line in 'mine' and nine in 'not mine'. Classic. Source: Enchiridion 1 (George Long's translation, public domain), in our words.

issues: Day 2 must open with the real reply count; never estimate it
Quiz is a soft question on purpose: the reveal splits the answer

scripts.hook: A teacher spent years trying to lose his students.
scripts.hook_b: His lectures failed if you clapped.
cards: A teacher spent years trying to lose his students.
He tried to talk new students out of it. On purpose.
If you only praised his lecture, he'd spoken for nothing.

A lame, formerly enslaved student.
Epictetus.
He tried to lose him. The world still reads him.
Send this to the teacher who never let you off easy.
scripts.visual: Public-domain engraving of Epictetus (Wikimedia Commons, credited in caption) behind the reveal card; colour flip Slate → Bone at the reveal. V1 otherwise.
scripts.caption:
Musonius Rufus judged a lecture a failure if his students only praised it, and he tried to put new students off, as a test of who would come back.

One who came back had been enslaved in Rome and walked with a limp. His name was Epictetus, and nearly 2,000 years later people still read his notes.

Who was the teacher who never let you off easy?

Sources: Epictetus, Discourses 1.9, 3.6, 3.23 (George Long's translation, public domain).

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Moodius: mine was a maths teacher who returned every page covered in red. I complained. I still check my working.

scripts.hook: A philosopher with nothing took in a baby nobody wanted.
scripts.hook_b: No wife. No money. One lamp. Then a baby.
cards: A philosopher with nothing took in a baby nobody wanted.
Epictetus. Formerly enslaved. Lame. Never married.
A friend was going to abandon his newborn.

Took the child.
Brought it up himself.
Idea: Simplicius, via George Long's introduction · Moodius words
He taught that we control little. He used it to raise a child.
Send this to someone who took in someone nobody else would.
scripts.visual: Hands folding a small blanket on a wooden table (owned b-roll, no faces), then Slate cards; warm Bone flip at the reveal.

source.author: Simplicius, as relayed by George Long
source.work: Introduction to The Discourses of Epictetus

scripts.caption:
Epictetus had been enslaved, walked with a limp and never married. An ancient commentator, Simplicius, records that late in life, when a friend was going to abandon his baby, Epictetus took the child and brought it up.

We only have this from a writer centuries later, so treat it as testimony, not a birth certificate. It's still a good one.

Who took someone in when nobody else would?

Source: George Long's introduction to the Discourses (1877), relaying Simplicius.

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Moodius: for everyone whose grandparent, aunt, neighbour or foster carer did this without making a speech about it.

issues: Ancient testimony, flagged as such in the caption

scripts.format: F4 Pep Talk vs Old Version
scripts.hook_b: Same bad week. Two pieces of advice.
cards:
A:
Visualise it going your way.

B:
Want it the way it actually goes.
A bets on the world. B bets on you.
The handbook doesn't need a vision board.
A or B? Comment one letter.
scripts.visual: Split layout: A in Ash on Graphite (deliberately flat), B in Bone with the Ember rule. Engine renders the two labelled cards in sequence; Remotion split screen only if switched on.
scripts.caption:
Version A is half the internet. Version B is from a handbook a student wrote down about 1,900 years ago: don't ask for things to happen the way you wish; wish for them to happen the way they do.

One bets on the world bending. The other bets on you bending a little.

A or B, honestly?

Source: Enchiridion 8, after George Long's translation (public domain), in our words.

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Moodius: I have a vision board. It's a list of bins to put out. B wins.

scripts.hook: That one friend who is late. Every. Single. Time.
scripts.hook_b: '5 mins away' (has not left the house)
cards: That one friend who is late. Every. Single. Time.
Epictetus had a two-word rule for this friend.
Can you guess the two words?
Idea: Gellius, Attic Nights 17.19, quoting Epictetus · Moodius words
Bear the wait. Forbear the lecture. Order them a drink anyway.
Send this to that friend. They'll see it in 20 minutes.
scripts.visual: Phone-chat mock-up rendered from text (no real chat, no names): '5 mins away' bubble, three dots, timestamp jumping 20 min. Then Slate cards.

source.author: Aulus Gellius quoting Favorinus on Epictetus

scripts.caption:
Epictetus's two-word rule, as a Roman writer heard it second-hand: bear and forbear. Put up with what other people do, and hold yourself back from the things you'd regret.

Applied to the friend who's always late: bear the wait, skip the lecture, still order them a drink.

How late is your latest friend, in minutes?

Source: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 17.19 (J. C. Rolfe translation), reporting Favorinus on Epictetus.

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Moodius: personal best wait is 47 minutes. I bore. I did not forbear.

issues: Positive, humorous, other-person opener: matches the reach-batch rules
